title: Evergreen Amusement Corporation v. Milstead
lead: Extra fill and delayed completion of a drive-in theater generated claims for payment and lost profits. Maryland’s highest court upheld the adjusted contract award and rejected the particular first-season profit estimate.
proceedings: Bench trial awarded unpaid price and extras less unfinished-work and delay allowances.
Maryland Court of Appeals affirmed with costs March 28, 1955.
limits: Chief Judge Brune dissented in part without a separate explanation. Court did not adopt a flat new-business profits bar or award the proposed $12,500. Exact net judgment not supplied.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The site contains less usable fill than expected
sections.cue: Original work and an added agreement
paragraphs: Evergreen Amusement hired Harold Milstead to clear timber, stumps, and waste, grade its drive-in theater site, construct a north-side drainage ditch, and install two hundred feet of pipe. The writing stated that additional fill would not be substituted for unsuitable on-site material at the stated price. Both sides assumed existing earth would balance cuts and fills. Their contour map was questionable because debris and trees could obstruct its preparation; the engineer regarded complete cross-sections as the accurate method.

That assumption failed. Even importing approximately eight thousand cubic yards did not complete planned grading. The parties agreed to lower the north side slightly to avoid more fill there. The trial court also found an agreement to pay sixty-eight cents per yard for outside dirt needed elsewhere. Evergreen denied it, but its president recorded pan-loads and approved the bill in writing.

sections.title: Payment and delay claims reach a bench trial
paragraphs: The trial court awarded Milstead the unpaid balance and extras, subtracting unfinished-work costs and delay damages based on rental value and actual expense. It rejected Evergreen’s anticipated-profit counterclaim. On appeal, Evergreen argued the outside-fill promise lacked consideration because Milstead already owed the work.

Judge Hammond’s Court of Appeals opinion upheld the promise on alternative grounds. The outside dirt cost more than the original price and reflected unforeseen difficulty and mutual mistake. Maryland’s exception to the preexisting-duty rule could apply even if precautions might have prevented surprise. Alternatively, the fill limitation either excluded that expense already or was ambiguous. If excluded, the promise purchased additional work; if ambiguous, experienced representatives’ agreement, records, and written approval persuasively showed their interpretation. Conduct could also establish modification.

Evergreen additionally offered a contemporaneous oral thirty-day completion promise. Even assuming admission was proper, exclusion caused no harm: both sides’ witnesses and the trial court treated thirty working days as reasonable, matching the legally implied time. Extra work, including a road needed for opening, had no separately agreed deadline. The court did not simply hold the oral term barred by the parol-evidence rule.

sections.title: The second season does not establish the missing first season
paragraphs: Evergreen claimed $12,500 profits lost from June 1 to mid-August. Its proposed expert had extensive experience building and operating local drive-ins, selling equipment, and assessing theater profits, and knew of a preselection demand survey. He would equate the missed first-season months with corresponding second-year profits, citing similar weather, population, and competition. Those were proposed assurances, not findings of equivalent actual demand.

The court upheld exclusion. An operating history could support reasonably certain profits, but a new enterprise presented greater speculation. It expressly refused a flat rule excluding all new-business profits; this particular comparison did not suffice. Local experience did not establish that an unknown new theater would attract the audience it gained after operating.

Earlier Maryland construction-delay decisions similarly involved uncertain returns. The federal antitrust cases Evergreen cited largely concerned existing businesses and conspiracies restraining trade, whose enforcement setting the court considered different. The court approved rental value and actual monetary loss as delay compensation on this record, rather than the anticipated $12,500.

sections.title: Unfinished drainage does not forfeit the price
paragraphs: Evergreen lastly argued any incompletion barred recovery. The court distinguished deliberate, willful breach from good-faith substantial performance, where price less deviation allowances could avoid giving the owner retained labor and materials without payment. Substantiality and justification ordinarily depended on facts.

The missing ditch and pipe represented about $1,000 of a job exceeding $13,000. The theater opened without them, and its president said the omission went unnoticed until afterward. Milstead said he had been told there was no hurry, left intending to return, and later feared nonpayment; he remained willing to finish with payment assurance. No clear error appeared in treating the work as subordinate, its omission as nonwillful, and a calculable deduction as adequate protection.

The court affirmed the entire adjusted judgment with costs. Chief Judge Brune dissented in part, but the report gives no separate writing or issue identification; no explanation for his disagreement can be assigned.
